title: Exercise 3.1: Meuse data. Co-kriging of cadmium using copper
text:
In this exercise you will apply the whole co-kriging workflow of Examples 3.1 and 3.2 to a new pair of variables:

Predict the concentration of cadmium (primary variable) in the Meuse study area using copper (secondary variable).
Compare ordinary kriging (cadmium only) and ordinary co-kriging (cadmium and copper) using prediction maps, their standard errors and cross-validation.
Analyse when co-kriging is worthwhile.

title: Exercise 3.1: Meuse data. Co-kriging of cadmium using copper
text:
4.1 Exploratory analysis
Plot the histograms of cadmium and copper, both on the original and on the log scale, and compute the correlation between both variables.

Which scale is more appropriate for the analysis?
Is copper a promising secondary variable to predict cadmium?







TipSolution






par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
hist(cd_sf$cadmium, main = "Cadmium", xlab = "ppm", col = "grey80")
hist(cd_sf$copper, main = "Copper", xlab = "ppm", col = "grey80")
hist(log(cd_sf$cadmium), main = "log(Cadmium)", xlab = "log(ppm)", col = "grey80")
hist(log(cd_sf$copper), main = "log(Copper)", xlab = "log(ppm)", col = "grey80")







cor(cd_sf$cadmium, cd_sf$copper)

[1] 0.9254499

cor(log(cd_sf$cadmium), log(cd_sf$copper))

[1] 0.8363329



As with lead and zinc, both variables are very right-skewed, and the log transformation makes their distributions more symmetric. We will work on the log scale.
The correlation between both variables on the log scale is high (0.84), so copper is a promising secondary variable. However, it is lower than the correlation between lead and zinc (0.97).

title: Exercise 3.1: Meuse data. Co-kriging of cadmium using copper
text:
4.2 Semivariogram of the primary variable
Compute the empirical semivariogram of log(cadmium) and fit a spherical model with a nugget effect. Choose the initial values by visual inspection of the empirical semivariogram.






TipSolution






v_cd <- variogram(log(cadmium) ~ 1, cd_sf)
vgm_cd <- fit.variogram(v_cd, model=vgm(psill=1.5, model="Sph",
                                        range=1000, nugget=0.5))
vgm_cd

  model     psill    range
1   Nug 0.5478481    0.000
2   Sph 1.3397973 1149.438

plot(v_cd, vgm_cd, pch = 19,
     xlab = "Distance (m)", ylab = "Semivariance",
     main = "Semivariogram of log-cadmium (Cd)")









Nugget effect \(\approx\) 0.55, partial sill \(\approx\) 1.34 and range \(\approx\) 1149 m.
The nugget effect represents about 29% of the total sill, much more than for lead: cadmium shows more variability at very short distances.

title: Exercise 3.1: Meuse data. Co-kriging of cadmium using copper
text:
4.3 Linear model of coregionalization
Create a gstat object with both variables, compute the direct and cross empirical semivariograms and fit a linear model of coregionalization.

Is the cross-semivariogram structured?







TipSolution






g <- gstat(NULL, id = "Cd", formula = log(cadmium) ~ 1, data = cd_sf)
g <- gstat(g,    id = "Cu", formula = log(copper) ~ 1,  data = cu_sf)

v <- variogram(g)
lmc <- fit.lmc(v, g, model=vgm_cd)
lmc$model

$Cd
  model     psill    range
1   Nug 0.5478481    0.000
2   Sph 1.3397973 1149.438

$Cd.Cu
  model     psill    range
1   Nug 0.1533914    0.000
2   Sph 0.5162377 1149.438

$Cu
  model      psill    range
1   Nug 0.08081862    0.000
2   Sph 0.24530645 1149.438



plot(v, lmc, pch = 19, col = "black",
     xlab = "Distance (m)", ylab = "Semivariance",
     scales = list(alternating = 1, tck = c(1, 0)))








The cross-semivariogram increases with distance and levels off at about 0.67: there is a clear spatial correlation between cadmium and copper.

title: Exercise 3.1: Meuse data. Co-kriging of cadmium using copper
text:
4.4 Predictions
Predict cadmium on the meuse.grid nodes using ordinary kriging and co-kriging. Plot the predictions and their standard errors for both methods.

Are there differences between both methods?







TipSolution






pred_krig <- krige(log(cadmium) ~ 1, cd_sf, grid_sf, model=vgm_cd, debug.level=0)
pred_cokrig <- predict(lmc, grid_sf, debug.level=0)

pred_sf <- grid_sf |>
  mutate(krig_pred   = pred_krig$var1.pred,
         krig_sd     = sqrt(pred_krig$var1.var),
         cokrig_pred = pred_cokrig$Cd.pred,
         cokrig_sd   = sqrt(pred_cokrig$Cd.var)) |>
  st_buffer(dist=20, endCapStyle="SQUARE")


tmap_mode("plot")

# Predictions
tm_shape(pred_sf) +
  tm_polygons(fill = c("krig_pred", "cokrig_pred"),
              fill.scale  = tm_scale_continuous(values = "brewer.yl_or_rd"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "log(cadmium)"),
              fill.free = FALSE,    # common colour scale
              col = NULL) +         # no cell borders
  tm_facets_wrap(nrow=1) +
  tm_layout(panel.labels = c("Ordinary kriging", "Co-kriging"))







# Standard errors
tm_shape(pred_sf) +
  tm_polygons(fill = c("krig_sd", "cokrig_sd"),
              fill.scale  = tm_scale_continuous(values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "SD (log scale)"),
              fill.free = FALSE,
              col = NULL) +
  tm_facets_wrap(nrow=1) +
  tm_layout(panel.labels = c("Ordinary kriging", "Co-kriging"))









Both prediction maps are very similar.
The standard errors of co-kriging are only slightly lower: the median standard error decreases from 0.917 to 0.914.

title: Exercise 3.1: Meuse data. Co-kriging of cadmium using copper
text:
4.5 Cross-validation
Compare both methods using leave-one-out cross-validation. Compute the mean absolute error (MAE) and the root mean squared error (RMSE). Plot the observed values against the cross-validation predictions for both methods.

Does co-kriging improve on ordinary kriging?
Why is the improvement so small, if the correlation between cadmium and copper is high?







TipSolution






# Ordinary kriging
cv_krig <- krige.cv(log(cadmium) ~ 1, cd_sf, model=vgm_cd, nfold=nrow(cd_sf),
                    debug.level=0)

# Co-kriging
cv_cokrig <- gstat.cv(lmc, nfold=nrow(cd_sf), remove.all=TRUE, debug.level=0)

cv_results <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Ordinary kriging", "Co-kriging"),
  MAE    = c(mean(abs(cv_krig$residual)), mean(abs(cv_cokrig$residual))),
  RMSE   = c(sqrt(mean(cv_krig$residual^2)), sqrt(mean(cv_cokrig$residual^2)))
)
cv_results |> mutate(across(c(MAE, RMSE), \(x) round(x, 3)))

            Method   MAE  RMSE
1 Ordinary kriging 0.664 0.901
2       Co-kriging 0.652 0.888



lims <- range(c(cv_krig$observed, cv_krig$var1.pred, cv_cokrig$Cd.pred))

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(cv_krig$var1.pred, cv_krig$observed, pch = 19, xlim = lims, ylim = lims,
     xlab = "Predicted (cross-validation)", ylab = "Observed",
     main = "Ordinary kriging")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "red")
plot(cv_cokrig$Cd.pred, cv_cokrig$observed, pch = 19, xlim = lims, ylim = lims,
     xlab = "Predicted (cross-validation)", ylab = "Observed",
     main = "Co-kriging")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "red")









Co-kriging slightly reduces both errors (the RMSE decreases from 0.901 to 0.888), but the improvement is very small. The observed vs. predicted plots are also almost identical.
The reason is that both variables have been measured at the same locations: wherever copper is available, cadmium is also available, so copper provides almost no new spatial information. A high correlation is not enough: co-kriging is most useful when the secondary variable has been observed at many more locations than the primary variable.

title: Example 3.2: Meuse data. Co-kriging prediction
text:
In this example we will:

Predict the concentration of lead (primary variable) in the Meuse study area using zinc (secondary variable), in the typical situation where the secondary variable has been observed at many more locations than the primary variable.
Compare ordinary kriging (lead only) and ordinary co-kriging (lead and zinc) using prediction maps, their standard errors and cross-validation.







TipR script



You can download the R script with all the code of this example and follow it step by step in RStudio:
 Download the R script

title: Example 3.2: Meuse data. Co-kriging prediction
section: Simulating the typical situation of co-kriging
text:
Simulating the typical situation of co-kriging
In the Meuse data, lead and zinc have been measured at the same 155 locations. To reproduce the typical situation of co-kriging, we assume that lead has only been measured at a random subset of 50 samples, while zinc is available at all of them.

set.seed(123)
idx <- sample(nrow(meuse_sf), 50)

lead_sf <- meuse_sf |> slice(idx)   # primary variable: 50 samples
zinc_sf <- meuse_sf                 # secondary variable: 155 samples






Sampling locations of lead and zinc.

title: Example 3.2: Meuse data. Co-kriging prediction
text:
4.1 Direct and cross empirical semivariograms
As in Example 3.1, we create a gstat object with both variables. Note that now each variable has its own data set: lead is taken from lead_sf (50 samples) and zinc from zinc_sf (155 samples).

g <- gstat(NULL, id = "Pb", formula = log(lead) ~ 1, data = lead_sf)
g <- gstat(g,    id = "Zn", formula = log(zinc) ~ 1, data = zinc_sf)

v <- variogram(g)
v |> filter(dist==0)

  np dist      gamma dir.hor dir.ver    id
1 50    0 0.01552923       0       0 Pb.Zn








ImportantZero-distance lag in the cross-semivariogram



The 50 lead samples are also zinc samples, so the cross-semivariogram includes pairs of observations at distance 0 (lead and zinc measured at the same location). This creates an extra lag with dist = 0, which must be removed before fitting the model (otherwise, fit.lmc() returns an error).



v <- v |> filter(dist>0)

title: Example 3.2: Meuse data. Co-kriging prediction
text:
4.2 Linear model of coregionalization

lmc <- fit.lmc(v, g, model=vgm_lead)
lmc$model

$Pb
  model     psill    range
1   Nug 0.1087290    0.000
2   Sph 0.4861717 1141.481

$Pb.Zn
  model      psill    range
1   Nug 0.07708997    0.000
2   Sph 0.56026925 1141.481

$Zn
  model      psill    range
1   Nug 0.07787233    0.000
2   Sph 0.64566000 1141.481



plot(v, lmc, pch = 19, col = "black",
     xlab = "Distance (m)", ylab = "Semivariance",
     scales = list(alternating = 1, tck = c(1, 0)))




Direct and cross empirical semivariograms of log-lead (Pb, 50 samples) and log-zinc (Zn, 155 samples), with the fitted linear model of coregionalization.

title: Example 3.2: Meuse data. Co-kriging prediction
text:
4.3 Co-kriging predictions
The co-kriging predictions are computed with the function predict() applied to the fitted gstat object (unlike krige(), which is designed for a single variable):

pred_cokrig <- predict(lmc, grid_sf)

[using ordinary cokriging]

For each node of the grid, it returns the predictions and variances of both variables, and the covariance between them:








Column
Meaning
Notation

Prediction of lead (log scale)
\(\hat{Z}_1(\mathbf{s}_0)\)

We are interested in the columns of the primary variable (Pb.pred and Pb.var).

title: Example 3.2: Meuse data. Co-kriging prediction
text:
Predictions





Predictions of lead (log scale) with ordinary kriging and co-kriging.










NoteInterpretation



Both maps show the same general pattern (higher concentrations near the river), but the co-kriging map is more detailed. In the areas without lead samples, ordinary kriging produces a smooth surface, while co-kriging uses the zinc samples to reproduce local variations. For example, the band of high concentrations along the river (in the north and centre of the study area) is much better captured by co-kriging.








Note



Predictions are shown on the log scale, the same scale as their standard errors. To obtain a final map of lead concentrations in ppm, predictions should be back-transformed with exp().

title: Example 3.2: Meuse data. Co-kriging prediction
text:
Standard errors

pred_krig$se <- sqrt(pred_krig$var1.var)
pred_cokrig$se <- sqrt(pred_cokrig$Pb.var)






Standard errors of the predictions of lead (log scale) with ordinary kriging and co-kriging.










NoteInterpretation




With ordinary kriging, the standard error is small only near the lead samples (triangles) and increases in the areas where only zinc has been observed (crosses).
With co-kriging, the standard error is reduced over almost the whole study area, also near the zinc samples. The median standard error decreases from 0.52 to 0.43.

title: Example 3.2: Meuse data. Co-kriging prediction
text:
Solution
Cross-validation errors with lead observed at all 155 locations:


            Method   MAE  RMSE
1 Ordinary kriging 0.295 0.402
2       Co-kriging 0.293 0.399


Interpretation:

When lead has been observed at all 155 locations, co-kriging hardly improves on ordinary kriging: the RMSE is 0.402 with ordinary kriging and 0.399 with co-kriging, whereas in the example (lead observed at only 50 locations) co-kriging reduced the RMSE by about 22%.
The reason is that zinc does not provide new spatial information: at every location where zinc is available, lead is also available. Co-kriging is most useful when the secondary variable has been observed at many more locations than the primary variable, as in the example.

title: Example 3.1: Meuse data. Direct and cross-semivariograms, linear model of coregionalization
text:
In this example we will:

Explore two spatially correlated variables: the concentrations of lead (primary variable) and zinc (secondary variable) in the Meuse soil samples.
Compute the direct semivariograms of both variables and their cross-semivariogram.
Fit a linear model of coregionalization, the joint model required by co-kriging.







TipR script



You can download the R script with all the code of this example and follow it step by step in RStudio:
 Download the R script

title: Example 3.1: Meuse data. Direct and cross-semivariograms, linear model of coregionalization
section: Log transformation of lead and zinc variables
text:
Log transformation of lead and zinc variables
Heavy metal concentrations usually have very right-skewed distributions: many low values and a few very high ones.

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
hist(meuse_sf$lead, main = "Lead", xlab = "ppm", col = "grey80")
hist(meuse_sf$zinc, main = "Zinc", xlab = "ppm", col = "grey80")
hist(log(meuse_sf$lead), main = "log(Lead)", xlab = "log(ppm)", col = "grey80")
hist(log(meuse_sf$zinc), main = "log(Zinc)", xlab = "log(ppm)", col = "grey80")








We will work with both variables on the log scale because:

The log transformation makes their distributions approximately symmetric.
The empirical semivariogram is based on squared differences, so it is very sensitive to extreme values. The log transformation stabilizes it.
Co-kriging is based on linear relationships between the variables, and on the log scale the relationship between lead and zinc is slightly more linear.
Both variables are on the same scale, which makes the sills of the cross-semivariogram easier to interpret.







Note



Predictions obtained on the log scale must be back-transformed with exp(). This back-transformation approximately gives the median, not the mean, on the original scale.

title: Example 3.1: Meuse data. Direct and cross-semivariograms, linear model of coregionalization
text:
4.1 Empirical semivariogram

v_lead <- variogram(log(lead) ~ 1, meuse_sf)
v_lead

    np       dist     gamma dir.hor dir.ver   id
1   57   79.29244 0.1046520       0       0 var1
2  299  163.97367 0.1965929       0       0 var1
3  419  267.36483 0.2507668       0       0 var1
4  457  372.73542 0.3330690       0       0 var1
5  547  478.47670 0.3875716       0       0 var1
6  533  585.34058 0.4817750       0       0 var1
7  574  693.14526 0.5031432       0       0 var1
8  564  796.18365 0.5545787       0       0 var1
9  589  903.14650 0.5693882       0       0 var1
10 543 1011.29177 0.6098806       0       0 var1
11 500 1117.86235 0.6253271       0       0 var1
12 477 1221.32810 0.5126165       0       0 var1
13 452 1329.16407 0.5755737       0       0 var1
14 457 1437.25620 0.4676728       0       0 var1
15 415 1543.20248 0.4804887       0       0 var1



The term ~ 1 in the formula means a constant mean (no trend).
By default, the maximum distance (cutoff) is one third of the diagonal of the bounding box of the data, divided into 15 distance lags (width = cutoff/15).

Remember: each row of the output corresponds to a distance lag








Column
Meaning
Notation




np
Number of pairs of observations in the lag
\(\lvert N(h)\rvert\)


dist
Mean distance of these pairs (m)
\(h\)


gamma
Empirical semivariance
\(\hat\gamma(h)\)









NoteInterpretation



For example, the first row indicates that there are 57 pairs of samples separated by a mean distance of 79 m, with an empirical semivariance of 0.105.

title: Example 3.1: Meuse data. Direct and cross-semivariograms, linear model of coregionalization
text:
4.2 Fitted theoretical model

vgm_lead <- fit.variogram(v_lead, model=vgm(psill=0.5, model="Sph",
                                            range=1000, nugget=0.05))
vgm_lead

  model      psill    range
1   Nug 0.05156252   0.0000
2   Sph 0.51530678 965.1506


The function vgm() defines a theoretical model with initial values for its parameters (chosen by visual inspection):








Argument
Meaning
Notation




model = "Sph"
Spherical model
—


psill = 0.5
Partial sill
\(\sigma^2\)


range = 1000
Range (for the spherical model, the exact range)
\(\rho\)


nugget = 0.05
Nugget effect
\(\tau^2\)



The function fit.variogram() then fits the model to the empirical semivariogram by weighted least squares (Chapter 2).






NoteInterpretation of the fitted model




Nugget effect: \(\tau^2 \approx\) 0.052.
Partial sill: \(\sigma^2 \approx\) 0.515.
Total sill: \(\tau^2+\sigma^2 \approx\) 0.567. The nugget effect represents about 9% of the total sill: the variability at very short distances is small.
Range: \(\rho \approx\) 965 m. Beyond this distance, lead concentrations in two samples are no longer correlated.




plot(v_lead, vgm_lead, pch = 19,
     xlab = "Distance (m)", ylab = "Semivariance",
     main = "Semivariogram of log-lead (Pb)")

title: Example 3.1: Meuse data. Direct and cross-semivariograms, linear model of coregionalization
text:
Plot of the fitted model

plot(v, lmc, pch = 19, col = "black",
     xlab = "Distance (m)", ylab = "Semivariance",
     scales = list(alternating = 1, tck = c(1, 0)))




Direct and cross empirical semivariograms of log-lead (Pb) and log-zinc (Zn), with the fitted linear model of coregionalization.




In each panel, the points are the empirical semivariograms (computed with variogram()) and the lines are the fitted linear model of coregionalization (fit.lmc()).






NoteInterpretation



The cross-semivariogram shows a clear spatial structure, very similar to that of the direct semivariograms: it increases with distance and levels off at about 0.59. This indicates a strong spatial correlation between both metals, so zinc can provide useful information to predict lead in co-kriging.

title: Example 3.1: Meuse data. Direct and cross-semivariograms, linear model of coregionalization
text:
Solution












Table 1: Comparison of the linear models of coregionalization for lead and zinc (example) and lead and organic matter (exercise).











Example (Pb and Zn)
Exercise (Pb and OM)




Number of samples
155
153


Correlation at the same sampling points (log scale)
0.97
0.53


Common range
\(\approx\) 965 m
\(\approx\) 1028 m


Cross-semivariogram sill: nugget effect
0.048
0.002


Cross-semivariogram sill: spherical model
0.544
0.227


Total sill of the cross-semivariogram
\(\approx\) 0.59
\(\approx\) 0.23






Interpretation:

The cross-semivariogram between lead and organic matter is structured: it increases with distance and levels off, so there is a spatial correlation between both variables.
However, this correlation is considerably weaker than with zinc (Table 1): the sill of the cross-semivariogram is much lower (\(0.23\) vs. \(0.59\)), and the correlation at the same sampling points is also lower (\(0.53\) vs. \(0.97\)). For the nugget effect component, the cross-semivariogram sill is almost zero: at very short distances, the variations of both variables are practically independent.
Conclusion for co-kriging: zinc is a much better secondary variable to predict lead. Organic matter could provide some information, but less.

title: Example 3.3: Navarre weather stations. Co-kriging of maximum temperature
text:
In this example we will:

Predict the maximum temperature (primary variable) in Navarre on 6 February 2010 using the minimum temperature (secondary variable) recorded at the same weather stations.
Compare ordinary kriging and ordinary co-kriging using prediction maps, their standard errors and cross-validation.
Learn how to compare both methods fairly.







TipR script



You can download the R script with all the code of this example and follow it step by step in RStudio:
 Download the R script

title: Example 3.3: Navarre weather stations. Co-kriging of maximum temperature
section: Boundary of Navarre and prediction grid
text:
Boundary of Navarre and prediction grid
We obtain the boundary of Navarre with the function esp_get_prov() and transform it to the same coordinate reference system as the stations:

Navarra <- esp_get_prov(prov = "Navarra") |>
  st_transform(crs = 25830)

The prediction grid is a regular grid of points every 1 km covering Navarre. The function st_make_grid() creates the grid over the bounding box of the boundary, and st_filter() keeps only the points inside Navarre:

grid_sf <- st_make_grid(Navarra, cellsize = 1000, what = "centers") |>
  st_as_sf() |>
  st_filter(Navarra)

nrow(grid_sf)

[1] 10381


We can check the result by drawing the boundary of Navarre, the nodes of the prediction grid and the weather stations:

tmap_mode("plot")

tm_shape(Navarra) + tm_borders(lwd=1.5) +
  tm_shape(grid_sf) + tm_dots(fill="grey", size=0.02) +
  tm_shape(stations_sf) + tm_dots(fill="red", size=0.5) +
  tm_add_legend(type = "symbols",
                labels = c("Grid nodes (1 km)", "Weather stations"),
                fill = c("grey", "red"),
                size = c(0.2, 0.5)) +
  tm_title("Prediction grid") +
  tm_layout(legend.position = c("left", "bottom"))









Each tm_shape() adds a new layer on top of the previous ones: first the boundary of Navarre, then the grid nodes and finally the stations.

The prediction grid covers the whole territory, while the stations are irregularly distributed: there are more stations in the north and fewer in the south and in the Pyrenees (north-east).





Maximum and minimum temperatures (ºC) recorded at the weather stations on 6 February 2010, classified by quintiles.

title: Example 3.3: Navarre weather stations. Co-kriging of maximum temperature
text:
Relationship between both variables

r <- cor(stations$TMAX, stations$TMIN)

plot(stations$TMIN, stations$TMAX, pch = 19,
     xlab = "TMIN (ºC)", ylab = "TMAX (ºC)",
     main = paste("Correlation:", round(r, 2)))
abline(lm(TMAX ~ TMIN, data = stations), col = "red", lwd = 2)














NoteInterpretation



The correlation between the maximum and minimum temperatures is weak (0.25). Moreover, both variables have been measured at the same stations. According to Example 3.2 and its exercise, we should not expect a large improvement from co-kriging in this situation.


Both temperatures have approximately symmetric distributions, so we will work on the original scale (ºC).

title: Example 3.3: Navarre weather stations. Co-kriging of maximum temperature
text:
5.1 Linear model of coregionalization

g <- gstat(NULL, id = "TMAX", formula = TMAX ~ 1, data = stations_sf)
g <- gstat(g,    id = "TMIN", formula = TMIN ~ 1, data = stations_sf)

v <- variogram(g, width = 10000)
lmc <- fit.lmc(v, g, model=vgm_tmax)
lmc$model

$TMAX
  model     psill    range
1   Nug  1.110432      0.0
2   Sph 11.228098 126421.1

$TMAX.TMIN
  model       psill    range
1   Nug 0.001538718      0.0
2   Sph 3.755327411 126421.1

$TMIN
  model    psill    range
1   Nug 1.435239      0.0
2   Sph 9.405934 126421.1



plot(v, lmc, pch = 19, col = "black",
     xlab = "Distance (m)", ylab = "Semivariance",
     scales = list(alternating = 1, tck = c(1, 0)))




Direct and cross empirical semivariograms of the maximum (TMAX) and minimum (TMIN) temperatures, with the fitted linear model of coregionalization.










NoteInterpretation



The cross-semivariogram shows some spatial structure, but its sill (3.76) is much smaller than the sills of the direct semivariograms (12.34 and 10.84): the spatial correlation between both temperatures is weak.

title: Example 3.3: Navarre weather stations. Co-kriging of maximum temperature
text:
5.2 Co-kriging predictions

pred_cokrig <- predict(lmc, grid_sf, debug.level=0)

title: Example 3.3: Navarre weather stations. Co-kriging of maximum temperature

Predictions

tm_shape(pred_sf) +
  tm_polygons(fill = c("krig_pred", "cokrig_pred"),
              fill.scale  = tm_scale_continuous(values = "brewer.yl_or_rd"),

Standard errors

tm_shape(pred_sf) +
  tm_polygons(fill = c("krig_sd", "cokrig_sd"),
              fill.scale  = tm_scale_continuous(values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "SD (ºC)"),

NoteInterpretation




Both prediction maps are almost identical: higher maximum temperatures in the south (Ribera) and in the low valleys of the far north, and lower in the mountainous areas, especially the Pyrenees (north-east). This pattern closely follows the altitude.
The standard errors are also very similar: the median standard error is 1.496 ºC with ordinary kriging and 1.494 ºC with co-kriging. In both cases, they are smaller near the stations and larger in the areas with few stations.

title: Exercise 3.2: Navarre weather stations. Kriging, co-kriging and universal kriging
text:
In this exercise you will replicate the analysis of Example 3.3 with data from another day, and extend it with a third method:

Predict the maximum temperature in Navarre on 20 February 2011 using ordinary kriging and co-kriging with the minimum temperature as secondary variable.
Predict it using universal kriging with the altitude as a covariate (Chapter 2).

Try to solve each task on your own before opening the solution.

title: Exercise 3.2: Navarre weather stations. Kriging, co-kriging and universal kriging
text:
4.1 Exploratory analysis
Compute the correlation of the maximum temperature with the minimum temperature and with the altitude.

Which of the two auxiliary variables seems more useful to predict the maximum temperature?

Compute the empirical semivariogram of the maximum temperature (with width = 10000, as in Example 3.3), fit a spherical model with a nugget effect, and predict the maximum temperature on grid_z.

v_tmax <- variogram(TMAX ~ 1, stations_sf, width = 10000)

title: Exercise 3.2: Navarre weather stations. Kriging, co-kriging and universal kriging
text:
4.4 Universal kriging with the altitude
Compute the empirical semivariogram of the residuals of the model with altitude (variogram(TMAX ~ Z, ...), with width = 10000), and predict the maximum temperature on grid_z with universal kriging.

What does the semivariogram of the residuals look like? Fit an appropriate model.
What does this mean?







Note



The covariate must have the same name in the data (stations_sf) and in the prediction grid (grid_z), so that krige() can evaluate the formula TMAX ~ Z at the prediction locations.








TipSolution






v_res <- variogram(TMAX ~ Z, stations_sf, width = 10000)
v_res

   np      dist    gamma dir.hor dir.ver   id
1  77  7375.017 1.310484       0       0 var1
2 257 15559.160 1.387442       0       0 var1
3 353 25239.802 1.149994       0       0 var1
4 407 35168.687 1.120912       0       0 var1
5 432 44814.346 1.244897       0       0 var1
6 435 54865.552 1.231796       0       0 var1
7 133 61592.035 1.090076       0       0 var1



library(lattice)
p1 <- plot(v_tmax, vgm_tmax, pch = 19, ylim = c(0, 5),
           xlab = "Distance (m)", ylab = "Semivariance", main = "TMAX ~ 1")
p2 <- plot(v_res, pch = 19, ylim = c(0, 5),
           xlab = "Distance (m)", ylab = "Semivariance", main = "TMAX ~ Z (residuals)")
print(p1, split = c(1, 1, 2, 1), more = TRUE)
print(p2, split = c(2, 1, 2, 1))








The semivariogram of the residuals is flat: the semivariance is approximately the same at all distances. Altitude explains the spatial structure of the maximum temperature, and the residuals show no spatial dependence. Therefore, the appropriate model is a pure nugget effect:

vgm_res <- fit.variogram(v_res, model=vgm(psill=1, model="Nug"))
vgm_res

  model    psill range
1   Nug 1.283103     0

pred_uk <- krige(TMAX ~ Z, stations_sf, grid_z, model=vgm_res, debug.level=0)







Note



With a pure nugget model, the residuals at different locations are uncorrelated, so universal kriging is equivalent to a linear regression of the maximum temperature on the altitude: the predictions do not depend on the nearby stations, only on the altitude of each location.

title: Exercise 3.2: Navarre weather stations. Kriging, co-kriging and universal kriging
text:
4.5 Maps of the predictions
Draw the maps of the predictions of the three methods.

Which method shows more detail? Why?
The highest station is at 1050 m, but some areas of Navarre are above 2000 m. Are the universal kriging predictions reliable in those areas?







TipSolution






pred_sf <- grid_z |>
  mutate(krig_pred   = pred_krig$var1.pred,
         cokrig_pred = pred_cokrig$TMAX.pred,
         uk_pred     = pred_uk$var1.pred) |>
  st_buffer(dist=500, endCapStyle="SQUARE")


tmap_mode("plot")

tm_shape(pred_sf) +
  tm_polygons(fill = c("krig_pred", "cokrig_pred", "uk_pred"),
              fill.scale  = tm_scale_continuous(values = "brewer.yl_or_rd"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "TMAX (ºC)"),
              fill.free = FALSE,    # common colour scale
              col = NULL) +         # no cell borders
  tm_facets_wrap(nrow=1) +
  tm_shape(Navarra) + tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(stations_sf) + tm_dots(fill="black", size=0.2) +
  tm_layout(panel.labels = c("Ordinary kriging", "Co-kriging",
                             "Universal kriging (altitude)"))









The ordinary kriging and co-kriging maps are very similar and smooth: they only use the information of the stations.
The universal kriging map shows much more detail, because it uses the altitude of each node of the grid: it reproduces the relief of Navarre (valleys, mountain ranges and the Pyrenees).
In the areas above the highest station (about 7% of the grid nodes), universal kriging extrapolates the linear relationship with altitude beyond the range of the observed data, so the predictions must be interpreted with caution.

title: Exercise 3.2: Navarre weather stations. Kriging, co-kriging and universal kriging
text:
4.6 Cross-validation
Compare the three methods using leave-one-out cross-validation (MAE and RMSE). Remember to compare ordinary kriging and co-kriging fairly (see Example 3.3).

Does co-kriging improve on ordinary kriging?
Why does universal kriging improve much more than co-kriging?







TipSolution






# Ordinary kriging
cv_krig <- krige.cv(TMAX ~ 1, stations_sf, model=vgm_tmax, nfold=nrow(stations_sf),
                    debug.level=0)

# Co-kriging
cv_cokrig <- gstat.cv(lmc, nfold=nrow(stations_sf), remove.all=TRUE, debug.level=0)

# Universal kriging
cv_uk <- krige.cv(TMAX ~ Z, stations_sf, model=vgm_res, nfold=nrow(stations_sf),
                  debug.level=0)

cv_results <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Ordinary kriging", "Co-kriging (TMIN)", "Universal kriging (altitude)"),
  MAE    = c(mean(abs(cv_krig$residual)), mean(abs(cv_cokrig$residual)),
             mean(abs(cv_uk$residual))),
  RMSE   = c(sqrt(mean(cv_krig$residual^2)), sqrt(mean(cv_cokrig$residual^2)),
             sqrt(mean(cv_uk$residual^2)))
)
cv_results |> mutate(across(c(MAE, RMSE), \(x) round(x, 3)))

                        Method   MAE  RMSE
1             Ordinary kriging 1.129 1.442
2            Co-kriging (TMIN) 1.104 1.427
3 Universal kriging (altitude) 0.898 1.163



Co-kriging hardly improves on ordinary kriging (RMSE of 1.427 vs. 1.442), even though the correlation between both temperatures is higher than in Example 3.3. The minimum temperature has been measured at the same stations, so it does not provide information at new locations: a high correlation is not enough.
Universal kriging clearly outperforms both methods (RMSE of 1.163), because:

altitude is strongly related to the maximum temperature;
altitude is known at every location, so it provides information where there are no stations.

When an auxiliary variable is available everywhere, it is better to include it in the mean of the model (universal kriging) than to use it as a secondary variable in co-kriging.
